https://www.politico.eu/article/vladimir.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin has given his government powers to temporarily manage critical infrastructure facilities if their owners fail to protect them against security threats. A decree published Monday gives Russia’s Federal Agency for State Property Management extensive powers to seize industrial sites if their owners have failed to take protective measures against uncrewed aerial vehicles, among other risks. It will operate seized businesses as the owner and Putin can designate any other entity as the temporary manager, according to the decree. Advertisement Advertisement Since launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Kremlin has stepped up efforts to bring privately owned assets — including industrial and defense-related companies — under state control. Around 805 companies were transferred to the state between 2022 and 2026, according to Vadim Yakovenko, head of the Federal Agency for State Property Management. “We are not talking about nationalization,” Russia’s First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov said in a press conference Tuesday , according to the state-owned news agency TASS. He blamed business owners for approaching threats “with varying degrees of responsibility.” In some cases, “ensuring the security of facilities and employees, unfortunately, is not a priority for them,” Manturov added. Critical businesses listed by the decree include fuel and energy facilities, industrial sites and logistics platforms. The decree comes amid intensifying drone strikes from Ukraine, including significant attacks on online retailer Wildberries and the country’s second-largest online marketplace, Ozon. A July report from the Ukrainian military said that its attacks have also disabled around 43 percent of the country’s oil refining capacity .

support for Ukraine after Russian drone strikes near Polish border Associated Press September 14, 2026 Last Updated: September 14, 2026 07:50 PM International News A locomotive damaged in a Russian drone attack is seen at Yahodyn railway station near Ukraine’s border with Poland on Sunday, Sept. 13. Ukrainian Ukrzaliznytsia Railway Company Press Office via AP WARSAW, Poland — NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Monday, Sept. 14, that Russian drone strikes near the Ukraine-Poland border — one of which hit a train shortly after senior visiting officials had passed through the same station — would drive the military alliance to increase its support for Kyiv, calling Sunday's attacks a sign of Moscow's growing desperation. The strikes “close to NATO territory” show Russian President Vladimir Putin’s “desperation and also his desire to sow fear and terror,” Rutte said at NATO’s political headquarters in Brussels. “Russia is growing increasingly reckless as it continues its terrible war against Ukraine.” Rutte pledged to increase support for Ukraine and bolster the 32-nation alliance’s own defenses along its long eastern border with Russia. “He thinks that he can stop us from supporting Ukraine and that he can undermine our unity. He is wrong,” the NATO chief said of Putin. Sunday’s strikes near the Polish border are the latest in a string of incidents that officials say point to a deliberate pattern of escalation by Putin as Moscow tests NATO’s response while pressing its offensive in Ukraine. Poland and Ukraine increase security cooperation along border Rutte's comments came as Poland pledged increased security along its border with Ukraine after a wave of Russian drone strikes near the frontier, including two that landed within kilometers of Polish territory. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned Sunday that Moscow appears poised to intensify its campaign against Ukraine’s borders with European countries. Ukraine is under mounting pressure from Russia’s intensifying air campaign that uses ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to pierce defenses. “These coming weeks and months will be a time of very intensified actions on the Russian side, and unfortunately we cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory,” Tusk said Sunday after a governmental security briefing in Warsaw. He issued a similar warning on Thursday. Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said Monday in a post on X that the Polish army recovered what was believed to be a Russian military drone from the Baltic Sea near the coastal village of Jaroslawiec. Polish officials said intelligence reports, including a CIA briefing last week, suggested Russia was likely to attack border points and intensify sabotage actions inside European countries as part of its efforts to discourage partners from supporting Ukraine. Tusk said he would consult NATO allies on preparing a potential joint response. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski underscored the alliance’s military edge in a social media post, saying that in the event of Russian aggression against NATO, European NATO air forces, without U.S. participation, would be capable of destroying half of Russia’s oil refineries faster than Ukraine. Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk described Sunday’s drone strikes as a serious escalation from Russia. He told broadcaster TVN24 on Monday that any spillover into European countries could take the form of sabotage or a sharp intensification of hybrid warfare “on a scale that we have not seen before,” or other actions along NATO’s borders. The warnings followed a strike Sunday on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border, minutes after a diplomatic delegation that included former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt had passed through the same station, according to Ukraine’s state rail operator. A second strike hit near a separate border crossing point between Poland and Ukraine. Kaja Kallas, the European Union's top diplomat, said Monday that the drone attacks near Poland's border were “clearly meant to scare Western countries from supporting Ukraine.” “We should show that we are there for Ukraine and we are not scared,” she said. Kremlin says Russia will continue strikes throughout Ukraine Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, asked Monday about the strike on the train near the Polish border, said Russian forces were operating “across the entire territory of Ukraine and continues to do so — and will continue to do so.” Peskov noted the potential role of Global South nations in a settlement, saying “any country can use its influence on the Kyiv regime to encourage it to show greater flexibility.” Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi each expressed willingness to help broker a settlement during recent meetings with Putin, who briefed them on the situation in Ukraine, Peskov said. Peskov also addressed U.S. President Donald Trump’s call for Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian diesel fuel facilities, saying “any call on the Kyiv regime to stop strikes on civilian economic infrastructure can only be welcomed.” Trump on Sunday called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure used to produce and distribute diesel, saying the attacks are causing a global shortage. He spoke after diesel prices in the U.S. hit a record on Friday , soaring past an average of $6 per gallon. ___ Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, right, speaks during a joint news conference with Poland's Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski in Kyiv, Ukraine, Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. Photograph: Matteo Secci/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Opinion Spain It shouldn’t take the eviction of an 87-year-old to get Spain’s housing crisis fixed María Ramírez Pédro Sanchez is an admirer of Zohran Mamdani. It’s time Spanish politicians emulated the New York mayor’s relentless focus on affordable homes Wed 30 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 04.38 EDT Share M aricarmen Abascal is a determined woman who uses a wheelchair to get around. She has needed her determination over the years she has spent fighting the real estate company that forced her out of her Madrid apartment last week. She had lived in the flat for more than 70 of her 87 years. Police forced their way into her apartment after a judge approved Abascal’s eviction . By then, protesters had gathered around the building, including the actor Carlos Bardem, Javier’s brother. Teargas was used against them. Abascal was taken to a Madrid hospital, suffering from anxiety and extreme exhaustion, while her supporters chanted: “You are not alone.” Demonstrations of solidarity with her and “all the other Maricarmens” have since erupted across Spain, with protest encampments springing up at Puerta del Sol square in Madrid as well as in Bilbao and Málaga. Thousands of people are evicted from their homes in Spain every year. In the first quarter of 2026 alone there were, on average, 44 eviction orders a day, mostly for disputes about rent. Behind those figures, cases involving single mothers and elderly tenants often come to light. But no eviction has sparked such a public outcry, a national protest movement and a call for urgent political action like the tale of Abascal. Evictions are actually in decline in Spain and are now about a third of what they were in the aftermath of the financial crisis. In 2014, there were more than 68,000 evictions compared with about 24,000 in 2025. Spain is one of the fastest-growing economies in the west. Employment and consumer data continue to defy the odds despite global economic uncertainty. But many young people and poorer older people surviving on pensions struggle to pay rent or buy a home, especially in the most prosperous cities. In Abascal’s case, the real estate company Urbagestión bought her apartment in 2018, ending her rent-controlled arrangement. Her rent was initially increased from €500 a month to €2,650, way beyond what her pension could cover. The Spanish supreme court upheld Urbagestión’s claim that the tenancy was invalid as it had been transferred twice, first to Maricarmen’s mother and later to her. But the original 1956 contract was signed by her father under Franco’s discriminatory laws against women . As Abascal lay in hospital, the company and her representatives reached an agreement , mediated by Madrid city council, for her to return home. The monthly rent will be similar to the amount she has paid for years, about €500 . This is a victory for the activism and solidarity of ordinary citizens who mobilised for a neighbour in need. But her case reflects how property companies, banks and hedge funds profit from vulnerable tenants and their once-affordable homes. It is also a reminder of the failure of politicians to protect the right to “decent and adequate” housing that has been enshrined in the Spanish constitution since 1978. View image in fullscreen Maricarmen Abascal, 87, is transported on a stretcher to an ambulance after being evicted from her apartment in Spain, 23 September 2026. Photograph: Susana Vera/Reuters The centre-left governing coalition has failed to change the law to protect the most vulnerable tenants from eviction, and to push through comprehensive housing reforms. On Tuesday, Pedro Sánchez’s minority coalition finally introduced a new housing bill that would ban evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, limit rent hikes for two years and ban investment funds purchasing houses for two years. Now the bill needs to be approved by parliament within a month. But Sánchez’s reliance on the support of a range of parties since 2023 has limited his room for manoeuvre. The socialist PM’s leftwing coalition partner, Sumar, had pushed for reforms to prevent cases such as Abascal’s. But Sánchez had shelved the proposals until now, fearing rejection in parliament. The latest uproar is forcing his hand, even if it means including tax breaks sought by Junts, a rightwing nationalist Catalan party. Madrid’s regional and municipal governments, in the hands of the conservatives, were slow to offer alternatives to Abascal until she was evicted, using the case instead to attack the national government. For the past three years, the Madrid regional government, led by the conservative Isabel Díaz Ayuso, has refused even to apply the existing national law to limit rent increases. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Spain’s highly decentralised system, with power divided at a local, regional and national level, is once again the perfect cover for politicians to do the minimum and blame each other while individuals suffer. Spaniards repeatedly identify housing as the country’s biggest problem, but the issue has not earned the intense political attention it deserves. A few days ago, Sánchez visited Zohran Mamdani, who is becoming a point of reference for the left in Spain and across Europe . Instead of trying to imitate the mayor of New York’s videos or his charm, fellow progressives could emulate his relentless focus on housing. Mamdani supports solutions across the ideological spectrum, from pushing for the construction of new apartment buildings to taxing real estate investment funds. He is supporting public housing and protections for tenants in rent-controlled apartments, but also working with private developers, even exchanging pleasantries with Donald Trump to advance a proposal for a large urban development project over Sunnyside Yard in Queens, New York. There are no magic bullets on housing. Fixing it will require hard work, smart planning, laser focus and an open mind. Winning progressive politicians have only now started treating this problem with the urgency it deserves. Will Abascal’s eviction prompt a new era in housing policy in Spain? If it happens, change will have come at a high price. It should not take the forcible eviction of an 87-year-old woman who just wants to remain in her home for the corrosive effects of unaffordable housing to be taken seriously. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwly.text: Image source, Azerbaijani social media Image caption, These schoolgirls were not allowed to enter classes because of their headscarves By Rayhan Demytrie Caucasus correspondent Published 4 hours ago "You are telling me, I can't come to school?" says a teenage girl in a navy blue Islamic headscarf, captured on video challenging a staff member at the entrance to her school. The footage has been shared widely on social media, and shows a group of girls in hijabs standing behind her applauding as she continues: "Why should I have to give up my religion?" Last Monday the education ministry in Azerbaijan began enforcing new uniform rules, turning away female pupils wearing hijabs. Protests began outside state schools in the capital, Baku, and in several southern districts including Masally and Jalilabad. Protests are rare in this oil- and gas-producing country of 10.5 million people. Azerbaijan is constitutionally secular and the government strongly enforces that. President Ilham Aliyev has been in power since 2003 and has little tolerance for dissent. Opposition politicians and many independent journalists are in jail. Azerbaijan is pulled between two neighbours, Turkey and Iran. Azerbaijanis belong to a Turkic group of nations, speaking a language close to Turkish, and Turkey is its closest ally. But like Iran to the south, Azerbaijan is mainly Shia - over 60% of its people identify as Shia Muslims, while most Turks are Sunni. The interior ministry said it had detained 37 people on Monday who tried to obstruct the rules and "grossly violate public order". Image source, Social media Image caption, Videos have circulated of protests taking place in and around the capital Baku The rules, approved on 21 September, ban clothing which contradict "the principle of secularism in education" in state schools. They do not mention the hijab. Similar guidelines were extended to teachers on 6 October. In one video, pupils outside School No. 69 in Balakhany, outside Baku, hold a banner reading: "The hijab does not prevent anyone from getting an education." Shahiza Huseynova, a mother who was protesting outside a school in the Mashtaga district of the capital, was detained on Tuesday. In an interview with Meydan TV, an independent Azerbaijani-language channel based in Germany, Huseynova's husband Agha said she had been given a warning: "Either you take off your child's hijab and send them to school, or you go to prison." Image source, Azerbaijan education ministry Image caption, An example shared by the Azerbaijani government of an acceptable school uniform under the new rules Friends have also lost contact with Ilkin Huseynov, an activist who on Tuesday launched an online platform called "Let Leyli Go to School". It offers free lessons from volunteer teachers to pupils barred from class. According to a friend, Huseynov left his home in Baku with unidentified men at about 16:00 on Wednesday, and his phone has been switched off ever since. The authorities have not commented, but friends believe he has been detained. On Thursday, the platform's Instagram page could not be accessed. Since the protests began, users have reported problems accessing Instagram and TikTok without a virtual private network (VPN). Most of the protests have been in religiously conservative neighbourhoods in Baku's outlying settlements and in southern districts near the 765km (475-mile) border with Iran. The authorities have long been wary of religious influence from Iran, where more ethnic Azerbaijanis live than in Azerbaijan itself. On the night of 13 October, Azerbaijan's State Service for Special Communications and Information Security said a "foreign hacker group" had attacked more than 100 state websites. A pro-Iranian group calling itself the 313 Team (Cyber Islamic Resistance) claimed responsibility. Azerbaijani officials have defended the rules. One MP, Nigar Arpadarai, told the 1news.az website that children did not choose to wear the hijab themselves but were influenced by their families. "A child has no freedom to choose a religion. This is a conscious prerogative of adults," she said. Azerbaijan pardons Frenchman after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire Published 23 September Azerbaijan and Armenia sign peace pledge at White House summit with Trump Published 9 August 2025 The row has now spilled over into Turkey, Baku's closest ally, which provided vital support during Azerbaijan's 2020 war with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh. The two countries call themselves "one nation, two states". President Recep Tayyip ErdoÄan, a devout Muslim, has spoken of creating a "pious generation". His chief adviser, Oktay Saral, has called the Azerbaijani restrictions "unacceptable" and urged Baku to "reverse this mistake". "A headscarf is not an obstacle; it is a requirement of one's faith!" Saral wrote on X. Several MPs from Turkey's governing AK Party joined in. Small demonstrations were held outside Azerbaijan's embassy in Ankara, organised by KÃ¶klÃ¼ DeÄiÅim, an Islamist movement linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, and outside its consulate in Istanbul, organised by conservative Islamist group ÃzgÃ¼r-Der. President Aliyev's New Azerbaijan Party accused Turkish officials of an "openly defamatory" information campaign and of "baseless accusations", warning that Oktay Saral's comments risked harming ties, and cautioned against interference in Azerbaijan's internal affairs. Earlier this month, Ilham Aliyev himself said no one should "stick their noses into our way of life". Behind the dispute there may lie another source of friction. Turkish protesters have linked the headscarf rules to Azerbaijan's close ties with Israel, which sells weapons to Baku and buys Azerbaijani oil. Turkey's relations with Israel have collapsed over Gaza, but Azerbaijan has tried to maintain relationships with both countries. That is a difficult balancing act. On Thursday, when Israel's President Isaac Herzog addressed a regional security summit hosted by Azerbaijan in Baku, delegations from Turkey, Iran and other countries walked out of the hall. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Tommy Robinson, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, arrives at Southwark crown court for the start of his trial. Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Tommy Robinson, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, arrives at Southwark crown court for the start of his trial. Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty Images UK news Journalists forced to flee homes after Tommy Robinson shared images of where they lived online, court told Far-right activist is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two MailOnline reporters Ben Quinn Mon 19 Oct 2026 12.36 EDT First published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 08.33 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Journalists and their family members had to flee their homes after “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics” were deployed by the far-right activist known as Tommy Robinson, a court has been told as his harassment trial got under way. Robinson, 42, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, was alleged to have targeted journalists from the Daily Mail and Mail Online by circulating images of their homes to millions of online followers and in effect encouraging them to join in making threats. He is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two MailOnline journalists, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber in 2024, which Robinson denies. Dirnhuber, a senior editor at the Mail, and his partner had to leave their home, while Young and his family were provided with a close protection officer after the alleged campaign of intimidation by Robinson. Robinson, a former member of the British National Party (BNP) and co-founder of the English Defence League (EDL), is accused of harassment causing fear of violence through X posts and direct messages. He is also alleged to have made a telephone call on 5 August 2024 in which he is accused of telling Young he would visit his house, saying: “I’m coming to get you.” Opening the case for the prosecution on Monday at Southwark crown court, barrister Ben Holt told the jury Robinson could have chosen to complain to a press regulator after the Mail reported on his alleged role as an “influencer” encouraging the violence that broke out after the Southport murders in July 2024. The paper’s coverage included photos of Robinson reclining on a sunlounger, a phone in hand, while on holiday in Cyprus, where a team from the Daily Mail had located him. Members of the jury were shown an image of a front page which included a photo of Robinson and the headline: “Stoking Race Riots from his Sunbed.” “This trial is about the defendant’s reaction to this, what he perceived to be, unnecessary intrusion into his holiday,” said Holt. “On social media, to millions of followers, he circulated images of their homes. His supporters, followers, got involved, threatening the journalists. Understandably, you might agree, they were scared, in some circumstances being forced to leave their homes. “That is what this trial is actually about. The prosecution say this defendant, using bullyboy, intimidatory tactics, threatened the journalists. He sent photographers to their home addresses. He put pictures, albeit redacted, of them out on his timeline on X for the enjoyment and appreciation of his followers. Holt took the jury through Robinson’s reaction on X to the Mail’s coverage, which was said to have changed in tone from being “reasonable” and “concerned” to “retaliatory”. Holt said that it was was inevitable “and would have been known” by Robinson that his online followers and supporters “would pick up the baton and attack” those he was talking about. Examples given included tweets from an X account using the name The Secret SpAd, which posted the home address of Young while the journalist was still in Cyprus. It was posted with the comment: ”Please be sure to congratulate him.” When Young returned home from Cyprus on 6 August, his wife and daughters told him that a man in a grey Audi had parked outside their home. The man was confronted by the journalist’s daughter but ignored her, and a report was made to police. A further report was made of a man sitting under a tree, pointing his camera at the house. Holt told the court: “Mr Young was concerned. His main concern was that while (Robinson) himself might not harm him, one of his many supporters online may seek revenge on him or his family.” The court heard that a third journalist who was involved the mail’s coverage, George Odling, also felt the need to leave his family home after becoming concerned with the publicity surrounding his colleagues. Ted Verity, the editor-in-chief of the newspaper, provided evidence to police of a voicemail he received from an individual who identified himself as Tommy Robinson, who allegedly told him: “I’ve already located every fucking one of you.” A video posted by Robinson’s X account was also played to the court, in which he accused the Mail of having “doxxed” his family and children. In the video, he sad: “You broke up my family holiday. Is it fair that I do that to you? You know I know the locations to where you are. To any other journalist, I will find you. So please, think: is it right?” The trial was adjourned until Tuesday morning.
